title: The state pattern, two ways
summary: The blog-post workflow implemented with the object-oriented state pattern using Box<dyn State> and self: Box<Self>, its trade-offs, and the Rust-flavored alternative that encodes states as types so invalid transitions do not compile.

blocks.md:
The **state pattern** is an object-oriented design pattern: a value has an internal state, represented by one of several **state objects**, and its behavior changes with the state. Each state object decides which state comes next.

*The Rust Programming Language*'s example is a blog post workflow:

1. A post starts as an empty **draft**.
2. When the draft is done, a **review** is requested.
3. When the post is **approved**, it is published.
4. Only published posts return their content; drafts and posts under review return an empty string.

blocks.title: The object-oriented version
blocks.md: `Post` holds a `Box<dyn State>` inside an `Option`. Each state type implements `State`, whose transition methods take **`self: Box<Self>`**: they consume the current state and return the next one. The `Option` lets `Post` take the old state out (leaving `None` for a moment) before putting the new one in.

blocks.output:
draft: ""
in review: ""
published: "I ate a salad for lunch today"
blocks.explain: `content` has a default in the trait that returns `""`; only `Published` overrides it. Its lifetime annotation says the returned text borrows from the `post`, not from the state.

blocks.title: Why self: Box<Self>?
blocks.md: The method is only valid on a `Box` holding the type, and it **takes ownership** of the box. The old state is consumed and cannot be used again, which is exactly what a transition means. It also explains the `Option`: Rust does not allow a struct field to be empty, so `take()` swaps in `None` while the transition runs.

blocks.title: Evaluating the pattern
blocks.md:
**Strengths:** `Post` knows nothing about the individual states. Adding a state means adding a type; the transition rules live inside the states.

**Weaknesses:** the states are coupled to each other (`PendingReview` must know `Published`); several methods are duplicated (`request_review` returning `self` everywhere); and **invalid transitions are silently ignored at run time**. Calling `approve` on a draft does nothing, and you only find out by testing.

Rust can do better by putting the states into the **type system**.

blocks.title: States as types
blocks.md: Instead of one `Post` type with a hidden state, use a **different type per state**. Each transition consumes one type and returns another:

blocks.output: I ate a salad for lunch today
blocks.explain: `DraftPost` has no `content` method at all, so reading a draft's content is a **compile error**, not an empty string. `approve` exists only on `PendingReviewPost`. Each transition takes `self` by value, so the old state is gone; shadowing (`let post = ...`) keeps the variable name.

blocks.title: Two designs compared
rows: a new type after each step
add a type; callers' code changes
a heap allocation and dynamic dispatch
states chosen by data at run time (from a database, a file)
workflows fixed by the program's logic

blocks.title: Rust's lesson, not a rule
blocks.md: Object-oriented patterns work in Rust, but they are not always the best fit. Moving checks from run time into types is one of Rust's strengths: "make invalid states unrepresentable". Comprehensive Rust calls this the **type-state** pattern; libraries use it for builders, file handles that must be opened before reading, and network protocols.

blocks.title: A type-state door
blocks.md: Model a door with three types: `Closed`, `Open` and `Locked`. `Closed` can `open()` or `lock(code)`; `Open` can `close()`; `Locked` can `unlock(code)`, which returns `Result<Closed, Locked>` (the wrong code keeps it locked). Uncomment the last line in `main` afterwards and read the compile error: an open door has no `lock` method.
blocks.expected_output:
opened
closed
locked
wrong code
unlocked
hints: Each method takes `self` by value and returns the next state type.
`fn unlock(self, code: u32) -> Result<Closed, Locked> { if code == self.code { Ok(Closed) } else { Err(self) } }`

blocks.title: The blog workflow, extended
blocks.goal: Extend the state-object design with new rules, and implement the same workflow as type-state.
blocks.behavior:
Part 1, state objects (`pub struct Post`, built on a private `trait State` with `Box<dyn State>`):
- `Post::new()`, `add_text(&mut self, &str)` (only works in `Draft`: in other states it does nothing), `content(&self) -> &str` (`""` unless published), `request_review`, `approve`, `reject`, and `status(&self) -> &'static str` (`"draft"`, `"pending"`, `"published"`).
- **Two approvals** are needed: the first `approve` keeps the post pending (but counts), the second publishes it.
- `reject` sends a pending post back to draft and resets the approval count.

Part 2, type-state: `pub struct Draft`, `pub struct Pending`, `pub struct Published`, each holding `content: String`:
- `Draft::new() -> Draft`, `Draft::add_text(&mut self, &str)`, `Draft::request_review(self) -> Pending`;
- `Pending::approve(self) -> Published`, `Pending::reject(self) -> Draft`;
- `Published::content(&self) -> &str`.
hints: Give `Pending` (the state struct) an `approvals: u32` field: `approve` returns `Box::new(Pending { approvals: 1 })` or `Box::new(Published {})`.
Add `fn add_text<'a>(&self, post_content: &mut String, text: &str)`? Simpler: give `State` a method `fn can_edit(&self) -> bool { false }` that `Draft` overrides, and check it in `Post::add_text`.
Add `fn status(&self) -> &'static str;` to the trait.
Name clash: inside the module, the state-object structs and the type-state structs need different names, for example `DraftState` and `PendingState` for part 1.
blocks.solution_explain: The state-object version absorbed two new rules without changing `Post`'s public API, but its invalid transitions are still silent. In the type-state version, editing a pending post or reading a draft's content cannot even be written. A two-approval rule in type-state would need a `PendingOnce` type, or a run-time counter: types are best for rules known at compile time.

questions.q: Why does the State trait use `self: Box<Self>` for transitions?
options: So the method takes ownership of the boxed state and the old state cannot be reused
questions.explanation: A transition consumes the old state.

questions.q: Why is `state` an `Option<Box<dyn State>>` rather than `Box<dyn State>`?
options: A post may have no state forever
take() needs something to leave behind while the old state is moved out
questions.explanation: Fields cannot be temporarily empty otherwise.

questions.q: In the state-object version, what happens when you call approve on a draft?
options: Nothing; the call is silently ignored
questions.explanation: That is the pattern's main weakness.

questions.q: In the type-state version, what happens if you call content() on a DraftPost?
options: Compile error: DraftPost has no content method

questions.q: When is the state-object design the better choice?
options: When the state comes from data at run time, such as a database record
When there are only two states
questions.explanation: Types cannot depend on run-time values.

points: The state pattern stores a `Box<dyn State>`; transitions take `self: Box<Self>` and return the next state.
It keeps `Post` simple but ignores invalid transitions at run time.
Type-state uses a type per state and `self`-consuming transitions, so invalid transitions do not compile.
Choose by where the state comes from: run-time data favors objects, program logic favors types.

terms.def: A design pattern where a value's behavior depends on an internal state object that decides the next state.
A method receiver that requires and consumes a boxed value.
Encoding the states of a value as distinct types so that only valid operations and transitions compile.
